text: And today, we’re going to answer these three questions.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: How a coronavirus attacks your body.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: How your body fights back.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: SOUND 3

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And how actually we scientists can give you a vaccine to help your body fight back.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Where should we start?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok so let’s start here

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: First, your body is made of lots of cells that are basically little factories that make all sorts of things that the body needs. And they’re usually all locked up tight, so nothing messes them up, right?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And I guess the virus is trying to break into our body’s cells, to… to get into our little factories?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Absolutely.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: How does the virus get into the cell?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Why don’t we go ahead and biggify the virus for you?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Okay...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: AH! <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Whoa that’s a HUGE virus!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, there’s orange spikes and a purple rim and it looks like a sun.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So those spikes are like a key that unlocks the cells in your body. In comes the virus. It’s like a little soldier on a secret mission.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It's just by itself. But once the virus can pick the locks on the cells, it can use all the machinery inside to make copies of the virus itself.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Then those copies unlock other cells and make more copies.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And eventually cells start getting destroyed. And that's why you start to get sick, because as the copies of the virus are made, the cells burst.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: How do we stop the virus?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: EQ CHANGE

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So, well, your body is not just going to let viruses come in and do whatever they want. Right? It’s going to try to fight back. And to do that, it starts making lots and lots and lots of little weapons.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And these little weapons called antibodies.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mhmm

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So this is the second thing I want to show you. Why don’t we actually biggify?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So these little antibodies that look like little V’s or little Y’s stick onto the coronavirus and they can cover up the spikes.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh yeah, I can see it happening now right over there… There’s the big spiky coronavirus blob and the antibodies are swimming over... why do you think they’re trying to cover up the spikes?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So that it won’t get into our cells and destroy our cells.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah so the antibodies, what they want to do is cover up the spikes

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So they can't work like a key. The spikes can’t fit in the doors of the cells. So the coronaviruses cannot get in.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: But it doesn’t seem to be working… the antibodies are kind of… slipping off the spikes. What’s going on?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Um, it seems as if the antibodies aren’t the right shape, so they can’t cover the spikes.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: These antibodies are a bust I guess! Maria Elena, do we need different ones?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yes, we actually have to get antibodies that are the right shape because the problem is for every different virus that comes in, your body has to make a new army of antibodies.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And that's really hard. Your body needs a lot of time to figure out how to make them just right.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And I guess if you get sick, you definitely don’t want to have to wait a long time to make antibodies. But what if our bodies could practice making them before we get sick, so it’s ready to defend against the coronavirus?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Absolutely. This is the third thing that I want to show you. It's what I do all day. I help make something called a vaccine, which is basically a fake, practice virus. It looks just like the virus, but it can't hurt you, so that the body gets a chance to practice fitting something on the spikes. And so here, let me actually show you how it's done. Let's biggify!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Now let's look at just the new vaccine.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It looks just like the virus!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Exactly. It's just got the same spikes. It sort of looks like a coronavirus, but because it's fake, it actually won't be able to break into your cells and hurt you.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Hmm

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So your body gets some time to practice and makes antibodies that would fit perfectly on the spike.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: That way, when the real coronavirus shows up, the body can immediately make the right kind of antibodies super quickly and then the real virus cannot get inside your cell.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Okay Mikah. We just learned a whole bunch of stuff about antibodies. You think you can help me recap to make sure we got it all?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: The antibodies are covering up the spikes, so it won't be able to use its spikes to get into our cells. But we have to have the right shape.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And how do scientists like Maria Elena help the body practice making the right kind of antibodies?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: By making a fake virus?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And that fake virus is called...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: A vaccine?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Exactly. But Maria Elena, it can’t be easy to make something that looks just like the coronavirus. What happens if things don't fit just right?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, if something doesn't exactly fit, we have to go back to the drawing board and try it again. And that's why it takes so long to make vaccines.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: SFX

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Hey what’s this? Maria Elena! Are you talking about science without me!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh hey! It’s the Experimoth!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I’m so sorry Experimoth! I just got excited about this and I forgot about you!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Experimoth. We were just talking about vaccines and the coronavirus. Do you know anything about experimenting with vaccines?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I know so much about experiments! I mean, I am the Experimoth. I was actually coming here to talk to Maria Elena about an experiment I’m planning to do. But she looks very busy. So maybe the two of you would want to come help?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok. Then if you could come this way,

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: SFX

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I'm going to take you to my home. It's called the Knock on Woods.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ooh...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok why don’t you walk and fly ahead, and I’ll meet you there after the break!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: [KIDS TAG]

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok, we’re back here on the Island of Explained. Mikah, you and I are here in the Knock on Woods with the Experimoth.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: What do you make of it? What do you think?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, it's really colorful. I see a lot of wood.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <Laughs> Some people think that the Knock on Woods is all about superstition…

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Hmm...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: But these knock on woods, they’re completely the opposite. So these are special trees that respond to each other.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Can you just knock on this tree over here for a second?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: That tree knocks, and then that causes the tree next to it to knock. And that causes the tree next to that to knock. And on and on and on and on and on!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh… so if you do something over here, it has an effect that spreads out across the woods!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Precisely. And that is what the Knock on Woods are all about. We try to figure out how one thing causes another thing.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Now, I brought you here because you want to know about developing a vaccine. And to do that, scientists like Maria Elena run experiments to figure out how one thing is having an effect on another thing.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Like if a vaccine is working to attack a virus!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Per...zzzactly!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I thought we could design an experiment together… but one that doesn’t involve people. It involves some bushes. My prize berrymint bushes…  full of amazing berrymint berries!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ooh...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Wow, you have hundreds of bushes. And those berries are wild!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: They kind of look like peppermints, but apples at the same time for some weird reason...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mikah, I love these berries so much, I’m basically obsessed with them. But I'm also really worried because look at this. Look at these leaves.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh my God. It looks like someone ate some of the leaves, and I don't know what those red dots are, but oh my gosh.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Those are red berry beetles. And they keep coming through and munching up all my plants.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mmm...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Look at this poor leaf. It's got more holes than Swiss cheese!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh, no.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: But there’s hope. The other day, this traveling snailsman left me a fancy voice message. Wait. Let me find it, I'll play it for you.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <SONG>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Slime, slime, snailsman slime.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: All you need is snailsman slime.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ten seconds with my snailsman slime

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And your berrymints will be just fine.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: (Slime!)

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: SFX

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ok, so if we listen to this snailsman, all we need to do is use the slime on my berrymint bushes for 10 seconds and the beetles should just go away. It sounds like a potential solution. Ya?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah. <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: But before we get too excited, here in the Knock on Woods, we like to experiment and see if a solution actually works before we go totally bananas with it. I was thinking that maybe you could help me design an experiment, like a berrymint experiment, to see if the slime works or not. Ya?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ya.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So what should we do to test to see if this slime will keep the beetles away from my bushes.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Maybe we can take the slime and put it on a leaf?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: That is a superb idea. But this is where you have to get kinda careful when you’re designing experiments.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It’s actually part of the reason they take so long! Because you have to make sure that it’s the slime that makes the beetles go away, and not… I don’t know, like a change in the weather! Or maybe the bugs get full and decide to go home!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So… hm.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Maybe we can get bushes and put slime on one of them and then put no slime on the other?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Why would you do that?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: We would see what's the effect and if it's fully the slime or if it's just something else.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Perfection! To make a good experiment we need to make sure that the only difference between our bushes is the slime. So we need to watch a bush that doesn’t get the slime just as carefully. In science we call this a control.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It’s basically so you can say “Hmm… what would’ve happened if I hadn’t done this experiment at all” and then compare.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mhmm.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Now… I think we’re almost ready. Mikah, is there anything else we should test here?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I think you should test more than one plant, just don't do all of your plants, so then they won’t all just die or something. You have hundreds of plants, right?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ya.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So if you put them on all of your plants, then all of them may or may not die! But if you just put it on 10... put slime on some and don't put slime on some, we would see the reaction.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Amazzzzing stuff. So we are going to put slime on ten plants, to see if it makes the beetles go away. But we are going to NOT put slime on the rest of my plants, so we can see what happens if we do nothing at all. Right?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Sure.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: All right. Okay. All right. And also okay. Mikah, are you ready to help me put this slime on some bushes?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It feels really slimy. It's also really sticky at the same time, like maple syrup.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It’s so disgusting! <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <Laughs> Yes. I mean. Oh, no.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: <Laughs>

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So can you help me count down because the snail that it was going to work in ten seconds, so we'll see.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Okay. Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: OK. This is the moment of truth. Mikah, let’s look at the plants that we did put slime on!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Wow. It looks beautiful. It doesn't have any bugs on it or holes…

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: This is really promising. But let’s make sure that it was the slime that made the bugs go away… So let's look at our control group over here. Remember these are the bushes that didn’t get the slime.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It looks the same disgusting <laughs> leaf with bugs on it. They look really, really hungry.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So if the bugs are still coming to the leaves without slime. But they’re gone from the leaves that do have slime on them...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mhmm...

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: EXPERIMOTH That means the slime is a solution!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Yeah!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Holy cow gee whiz! I am so happy that everything is solved! I’m going to put slime on everything!  I’m going to put slime on my socks. I’m going to put slime on my face!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Wait, Experimoth! Hold on. Look at the bushes now.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Sorry, what was that, Noam?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh, my gosh, what happened?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: It looks like the slime got rid of the bugs… but then it made the leaves all gross!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: They're yellow. Oh, my God. They’re just so disgusting.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Ugh. I'm honestly very grateful to you, Mikah. What if I'd put this on all of my plants?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Oh, they would have been dead.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, I’m sad to be losing ten bushes, definitely, but this is another important lesson when you're testing cures. Sometimes, they have side effects that take a little while to show up. And you always need to be sure that your experiments are safe.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Mhmm

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: I bet Maria Elena could actually tell you a lot more about all of this. And this is right about the time that we generally have an afternoon stroll. I wonder if—

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Hello Experimoth! It's time for our little science stroll. Where are you?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Maria Elena! Just the scientist I was hoping to see! We were just doing this experiment because my bushes had bugs, and then a snail gave me some slime that was supposed to drive them away in ten seconds! And it all reminded me of your work with vaccines. Except you’re trying to keep viruses away, not bugs!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, yes, but, you know, it's a lot harder than that.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: First, we need to find a big group of people to test on, which means that we have to find lots of people willing to be in an experiment! Then, we need to make sure that the vaccine actually works and that takes much, much longer than ten seconds to see, right?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: And just like you did, we also use a control. We give some of them a shot with the fake virus in it, we give other people a shot without the fake virus and then we watch them to compare to see what happens. But then, third, because we're going to be giving this vaccine to people—and healthy people—we have to make extra sure that they won’t develop any bad side effects over time. So we need to wait for a long, very long time.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: How long do you think we have to wait?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Well, we probably have to wait for at least one more year before we know for sure that we have a vaccine that can work fast and that it actually is safe for everybody.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: So Mikah, if your friends wanted to understand why it takes so long to get a vaccine, what would you tell them?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Because they have to do a lot of things before getting a vaccine, like they have to find the right antibodies, and then they have to make a fake virus, and then they might make the vaccine wrong so they have to do it again, because they don’t want anyone getting sick.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: That makes a lot of sense to me! And Mikah, I’m really sorry that I can’t give you a vaccine, but I would like to give you some berrymints to take with you back home! I hear they’re good with eggs… so maybe you can make eggs-berrymint?

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Thank you!

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Alright, Mikah. It’s about time to leave. But I’ll be back in two weeks with some more Island of Explained adventures. And don’t worry, it won’t all be coronavirus questions. We’ve got loads of fun stuff in the works.

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text:
K, bye!

MIKAH

episodeName: July 17, 2020; The Island of Explained: Vaccines
text: Alright, Island - I’ll see ya in two weeks!

And I think if everybody were wearing cloth masks when they're most needed, we may be able to make a real dent in what's going on right now. And of course, it's not a panacea. And we do need particularly public health infrastructure and testing and tracing to also make that impact. But masks can help.
How much can they help? Do we have any data that suggests the difference mask wearing can make?

Yep, places with high community spread, but also indoor public spaces where people gather.

I think in some places it is clearly a political problem. You know, in Georgia in particular, we've seen active interventions on the part of elected officials to make sure that mask mandates aren't happening. So it's not just leaving it up to localities to make the decision themselves. It's actually interfering with their ability to enforce a mandate.

Yeah, I mean, I wrote a piece about masks and particularly not just people who are who find them to be an inconvenience, which is understandable, but also people who are ideologically opposed. And I had a lot of people contact me and I talked to some of them about what's going on for them. And I think that they were very open to hearing what I had to say about why masks are worth wearing, simply because I hadn't kind of yelled at them in my piece that I wrote. And I think it was a learning moment for me that, you know, if you, as a public health person or as somebody who's trying to give in somebody in your community to wear masks, if you hear what their concerns are and you take the time to to acknowledge them, you can have a much more productive conversation.

And I think it does take more time. And I think some people see it as coddling to to engage with people who are ideologically opposed to masks or having a hard time wearing them. But actually, this is how public health ends up being effective, is acknowledging what people's barriers are or taking the time to understand them and then trying to figure out how we can overcome them both through our messaging and through interventions. So I would encourage people to take that approach rather than a shaming approach, which we know doesn't really work very well in public health.
So it's going to take a lot of conversations and it's still a conversation worth having.

episodeName: JULY 27, 2020 / RURAL AMERICA MEETS BLACK LIVES MATTER
text: Bethel is a town that's about a 45 minute drive from Cincinnati, Ohio. I think in some places people would think of it as like an exurb, but from what everyone has told me, it does not feel like that. It feels like a rural place.

episodeName: JULY 27, 2020 / RURAL AMERICA MEETS BLACK LIVES MATTER
text: This is Anne Helen Peterson. She’s a culture reporter for BuzzFeed, where she wrote about one fateful protest in Bethel.

episodeName: JULY 27, 2020 / RURAL AMERICA MEETS BLACK LIVES MATTER
text: So the town proper is 2,700-ish people. But then, you know, outside of the small village line, there are more people who consider themselves residents of Bethel. And there's the village proper, which is a downtown area that has been there since the early 19th century. And it has a bunch of churches. People say like there's about a church per person, but a lot of other things have been pretty hollowed out, like there used to be a normal grocery store and now it's a discount grocery store that doesn't have good produce, that sort of thing. And there's like a bunch of gun shops and pawn shops.

episodeName: JULY 27, 2020 / RURAL AMERICA MEETS BLACK LIVES MATTER
text: In early June, this substitute high school teacher, Alicia Gee, was seeing that there were protests organized in small towns all around her. You know, one thing she said to me was like, if Hazard, Kentucky can have a protest, then we can have a protest. But she was very deliberate about thinking through what kind of gathering that they wanted to have. They wanted it to be a demonstration in Solidarity of Black Lives Matter. They wanted to think of it as being a big tent to invite people who were all along the spectrum of, you know, ‘Defend the police,’ to, you know, ‘I just I support working towards equality.’ They wanted to go beyond just the handful of people that she already knew would be interested from, you know, her personal circle. So she decided to post it on the Facebook page that has kind of become a de facto community page since the local news has pretty much evaporated. And she was pretty scared about what would happen. And she waited until later at night and then, like, posted some information about it and then went to bed and woke up in the morning. And there were just a ton of messages and comments about like, ‘We don't need that here.’ Like, ‘How dare you bring that here?’ And a lot of it, I think, it's less to do with what the message of the protest was going to be and more to do with what people had seen largely on Fox News about what these protests were, which were violent conflagrations.

episodeName: JULY 27, 2020 / RURAL AMERICA MEETS BLACK LIVES MATTER

[MIDROLL]

Matthew, before the break, we were talking about how Democrats brought a plan to the table back in May, the Republicans offered one up on Monday, a few days before these unemployment benefits are set to expire. What were the Republicans busy disagreeing about?

Well, so the unemployment benefits has been a source of concern ever since it happened. And the way this worked was originally Democrats wanted to raise the generosity of unemployment insurance benefits so that people would get their sort of full paycheck replaced by the UI system. And then it turned out that state labor departments were not able to do that on a technical basis.  It's not how they're set up to work. So Democrats came up with this kludge, which was that they would just enhance benefits by six hundred dollars a week.  And that meant that on average, you would sort of replace 100 percent of lost wages. But in detail, it doesn't work like that. Mmm.

So Republicans are really hung up on this and they are very interested in making the program less generous. Now Democrats keep saying, ‘Look, like, what are the jobs that people are going to get?’ You can look at a million indicators, right? Whether it's wage levels, job openings, there's just no sign that there's a practical problem of unemployed people refusing to take jobs because the UI is so generous. And Democrats are saying, look, this bonus money it’s incredibly well targeted. It's going to people who are using the money to pay the rent, make ends meet. So you get money, you buy groceries, you go out. It keeps the economy going. But this isn't just Democrats versus Republicans. This is also Republicans versus Republicans?

Yeah, I mean, there is one set of Republicans who I think have become true believers on anti-stimulus politics.  Like what did Republicans say in 2009, 2010, in 2012, when President Obama kept saying, ‘We need to spend more money to keep the economy going?’ Republicans were saying back then, like, ‘No, spending money doesn't help the economy.’ So today, one bloc of Republicans is like, ‘Hahaha, we're hypocrites. Just to be clear here, is this more about, you know, you shouldn't be getting paid more to stay at home than your cousin who's going to work every day at Whole Foods? Or is it about we just shouldn't be spending this much money and adding trillions and trillions and trillions of dollars to the deficit?

Well, it's about both of those things, right? Because if you just had this worry about the incentives, that was the only thing you cared about. You could come up with a workaround. You know, you could say, ‘OK, we're going to give less money in unemployment insurance, but we're going to spend trillions of dollars on stimulating the economy through some other means. But Republicans don't want to do that, right? They want a small bill. So with a small bill, you would

say, OK, then we have to target everything hyper effectively. And that means being very generous to the worst off people. But Republicans don't like that idea because they think it damages incentives, so they're caught between the pressure to keep the overall costs down, but also to avoid being too generous to the poorest. And they've come out with a bill that's like a little bit neither fish nor fowl. And it just reflects those internal caucus dynamics rather than, I would say, an economic analysis of the situation.
So who holds the upper hand in this fight? Is it Democrats? Is it Republicans?

So by the oddball rules of Congress, who holds the upper hand depends on what Republicans do next. If McConnell can get all his people together behind this and get a majority for it, then he has a strong hand because Democrats are saying unemployment expiration is so terrible, but it will have already expired. So two hundred dollars is better than zero dollars. So really, why are Democrats holding off? Why are they stonewalling? Blah blah blah, blah blah blah. And supposedly Democrats will be under pressure to come down closer to McConnell's. And at that point, more vulnerable Senate Republicans like Cory Gardner or Susan Collins, they need to start saying, ‘Hey, Democrats, can we work a deal?’ This is like weird Capitol Hill stuff that it should all hinge on exactly how nutty does Rand Paul want to be?
<laugh>

So one thing they could do is quickly, you know, Wednesday or Thursday, put on the floor an unemployment extension for like three or four weeks, right? <Sigh>. All told, it just feels like the government abdicated its responsibility to handle this pandemic particularly well. I wonder I mean, as the rest of the world seems to be inching towards reopening and returning to whatever version of normal they can muster. Is the United States at risk of really falling behind here as cases continue to climb, states continue to re-shut down and the government fights over how to take care of people who are caught in the balance?

I mean, it's really embarrassing. I think if you look at the two parties, one thing you see here is that actual members of Congress who are Democrats are really into the nuts and bolts of governance. Or talking about whether there's too much violence happening in the Portland protest. You know, like like those kinds of things animate them. But when Republicans have the majority, the fact that it took them 10 weeks to bother coming up with this bill, it's just a signpost that a lot of their members are not that engaged with this kind of thing.

They weren't like, ‘Let's drop everything and figure out what we're going to do here.’ They kept kind of fighting or having vague positions. Some members worked very earnestly on this, but a lot of them didn't. And it's a big problem that the governing party in the United States is not that interested in this question.

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: So at the beginning of the pandemic, when we were first hearing about cases in China, the reports were about respiratory symptoms.

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: It turns out that SARS-CoV-2 which is the virus that causes COVID-19, affects a lot of your major organs, including your heart, your kidneys, your brain, even your nervous system and your bloodstream.

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: Yikes. Okay, well, let's take a deep breath and get into all that, starting with, I guess, the thing that most people are aware of, what's the lingering effects on people's lungs that we've seen?

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: So basically, you have all these gaps in your lungs if you think about them like a sponge. There are those gaps are supposed to be there. But when you're sick with COVID-19, those spaces can get filled with debris and pus. And so that makes your lung way less flexible. Normally, when you breathe, your lung expands like a balloon. And when it's filled with all this pus it can't do that. So in acute infections, that ends up looking like ground. You may have heard of people talking about ground-glass opacities, which is on a C.T. scan. A normal lung will look black and COVID-19 patients’ lungs look gray. So it's kind of unclear how much of that goes away once your acute infection is gone. And it's still too early to know how many of those are going to be permanent. But we can look back at other Coronaviruses that we know a little more about, like SARS and MERS, and studies on both of those coronaviruses suggests that about a third of patients have some level of reduced lung capacity for the long term. One of the studies actually followed patients for 15 years. So that suggests that some of this lung damage may be permanent.

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: Wow. Let's let's move on to the heart. What's going on with people's hearts and COVID-19. And how may those effects linger?

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: I know there is so much focus on a vaccine right now, but have there been any breakthroughs in treating all of these lingering symptoms from, you know, inflammation of the lungs to the heart, to the nervous system, to people losing their sense of smell and taste?

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: Yeah, there have been. There are a number of post COVID-19 clinics popping up around the country. Some of those treatments come from research on how to recover from being hospitalized generally with other diseases. We know that if you're intubated or ventilated or you're you're in an ICU, especially if you're there for a long time, that can have a number of different impacts on your body. For example, being in bed for a long time causes your muscles to deteriorate, which can make any shortness of breath feel worse. And there's also a significant emotional impacts of being so sick and worried about what's going to happen to you. A lot of people experience anxiety, depression, PTSD after being in the hospital. So we have research on what some of these impacts are like. And there are people who are working to help COVID patients get treatment for these kinds of symptoms.

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: I just feel like hearing about all these lingering effects really brings to light the fact that this virus is just no joke, irrespective of how confident or healthy or young you might be, because you may have lingering symptoms that last potentially for the rest of your life?

episodeName: 7.30.20 / Life after Covid-19, explained by Carl (who had it)
text: Yeah, I think, unfortunately, we have a lot of the conversation has been around whether or not you'll die if you get COVID-19. episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: [SCORING IN — APM BRIDGE TO TOMORROW]

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: The Bad Boys of tech came to Capitol Hill to testify on Wednesday. And by “came” I mean they logged onto Webex. But they were wearing suits and ties. And swore an oath not to lie.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Tim Apple. Mark Facebook. Billionaire Bezos. And Sundar Google.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: This is the Tim, Mark, Jeff, and Sundar Show. Here’s your host, Sean Rameswaram.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: [SCORING OUT]

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Casey Newton. You write about tech and democracy for the Verge. How big a deal were Wednesday's hearings? Nothing quite like this had ever happened before, at the very least, yeah?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: With the exception of the Microsoft antitrust case in the late 90s, we really haven't seen meaningful antitrust regulation in this country for 50 years. Thirteen months ago, the House Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee undertook an investigation into the market power of Apple, Amazon, Facebook and Google. And in the months since, they have held five preliminary hearings. They have produced one point three million documents. And Wednesday, we had the culmination of that. This hearing where you had the CEOs of the big tech companies facing real questions about how their companies have dominated the markets they're in.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: For people who couldn't watch, what did the main event look like? Because none of these dudes actually showed up, huh?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Well, as you know, Sean, we have a global pandemic that's happening right now.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <laughs> Sure.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text:
And so rather than risk it all to appear before the antitrust subcommittee …

SEAN

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And of course, Jeff Bezos appeared to have the nicest room because he has the most money by far.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And that is how that works. You make the most money? You have the nicest room. And that’s just basic science.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <laughs> So I didn't get to watch all of it, but I did get to watch some of it, including the opening statements in it, in which each one of the tech lords laid out their inspiring American billionaire business stories with these gentle sort of preemptive suggestions that nothing about Apple, Facebook, Google or Amazon was anti-competitive. It felt like foreshadowing.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yeah. I mean, nobody loves America like a billionaire, right? Things are going very well for them. And they believe very firmly that they have acted within all of the relevant rules and laws and that nothing ought to change.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <OPENING INTRO CLIPS>

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: We also know that customers have a lot choices and that our products face

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: fierce competition.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Many of our competitors have hundreds of millions or billions of users. Some are upstarts, but others are gatekeepers with the power to decide if we can even release our apps in their app stores to compete with them.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Research found that free services like search, gmail, maps, and photos provide thousands of dollars a year in value to the average American, and many are small businesses using our digital tools to grow.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Amazon accounts for less than one percent of the 25 trillion dollar global retail market and less than four percent of U.S. retail.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And of course, immediately thereafter, that sort of utopia they painted was pierced by the representatives on the committee. It was kind of like whiplash watching it because it would go from like Google and the military to like Facebook and free speech to like iPhones. So why don't we just help the people at home and go company by company, starting with Apple? Because Tim Cook seemed to sort of have an easy go.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: The thing that is happening with Apple is that it runs one of the two dominant mobile phone operating systems and it also operates an app store that is necessary to use any apps on that phone. And for many of the apps that run on that phone, Apple charges a 30 percent cut of revenue. And that is true even in cases where it makes a competing app that does not have to pay that cut. So, for example, Apple makes a music product that charges 10 bucks a month and Spotify makes music product that costs 10 bucks a month. Spotify has to pay three of those dollars to Apple. And so many companies have come forward to say that this is hurting competition because they are unable to invest the same amount that Apple is and that they're not able to compete.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And how did Tim Cook respond to that, that allegation that the App Store is inherently anti-competitive?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Tim Cook says that...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> TIM COOK: Eighty-four percent of the apps are charged nothing. The remaining 16 percent either pay 15 or 30 depending upon the, the specifics.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And he says, hey, if you don't like it, go find another operating system on another phone!

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: People have like a 50/50 option there? It's Apple or Google. Did Tim Cook sort of, like, get off easy in the whole thing?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I think Tim Cook got off easy. He got the fewest questions of anyone up there, something like 35 questions compared to something like 60 for Zuckerberg. So it seemed like members just were not as interested in scrutinizing Apple as they were the other giants.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And everyone loves to scrutinize Facebook, including you of course. the questions to Mark Zuckerberg felt sort of familiar, like old hat. Did they feel new and interesting to you?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: You're right in that Congress was really looking backward when it came to Facebook, whereas the antitrust questions facing the other companies feel much more current and future. with Facebook. The question was

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> REP. JERRY NADLER (D-NY): Mr. Zuckerberg, you have written that Facebook can likely always just buy any competitive start-ups. In fact, on the day Facebook bought Instagram, which you described as a threat, you wrote “one thing about start-ups is you can often acquire them.”

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And so they presented a bunch of new documents which we reported on at the Verge that showed conversations in which Zuckerberg says that it is a competitor and he would like to neutralize that threat. Now, Zuckerberg told Congress, look...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> MARK ZUCKERBERG: I’ve been clear that Instagram was a competitor, in the space of mobile photo sharing...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: But we never could have imagined it was going to grow as big as it eventually did. And in fact, as Facebook says...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> MARK ZUCKERBERG: By having them join us, they certainly went from being a competitor in the space of mobile photo sharing.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <laughs> Yeah, I saw that moment and I kind of scratch my head because I felt like Instagram was pretty huge before Facebook acquired it.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: It was certainly growing by the time that the ink dried on the contracts and now today it has over a billion users. So, you know, certainly Facebook had the data that showed that it was growing incredibly quickly and that growth has done nothing but continue ever since,

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Hmm. Google had a much tougher go, it seemed there were a lot of representatives taking a lot of Google's decisions recently apart.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yeah. Google faces the most imminent risk of real anti-trust action. There has been some reporting that an antitrust case may be brought against them by the federal government this summer. And a lot of it has to do with search results when you Google something. In many cases, you will not see what you used to see on Google, which was linked to Web sites. Instead, Google will try to answer your question for you. And often it will answer with another Google product. Right. Like if you search for a location on Earth, Google will show you Google travel products. And that has made it harder to compete for other travel based businesses. Right. Or if you think about local reviews, Yelp built a whole business on on reviewing local businesses. And it used to rank really highly in Google search. And then Google started to build in reviews of local businesses. And now Yelp reviews can be harder to find. So it's those kinds of things that have gotten regulators attention. And it seems like that has been persuasive to at least some of those regulators.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: So did Sundar Pichai do a good job of convincing the antitrust committee that Google is doing its best to foster competition? Or is the federal government sure to take action later this summer?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I don't think he did a good job convincing because I actually don't think that this hearing was about convincing anyone. It was much more of a forum for members of Congress to present what they had learned and to show the homework that they had done. It was rare for a CEO to get more than a few sentences out of their mouth without being interrupted and told to wrap it up.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> SUNDAR PICHAI: Congresswoman, most of the data we collect is to help users and provide personalized experiences back. Add da—

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: OK, thank you, thank you so much, Mr. Pichai. Mr. Chairman, I yield back.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: So in Sundar's defense, he didn't have a lot of room to make his case.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And of course, lastly, the other elephant in the room that is certainly facing a lot of allegations of being anti-competitive and was a big debut for billionaire Bezos. Is Amazon right?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yeah. He had never appeared to testify before Congress before, which seems wild, and he got questions about how Amazon's marketplace operates and whether it has made life difficult for the sellers that use that platform. Probably the the thing that got the most attention is that Amazon has been accused of analyzing the sales activity on its platform, saying what the other sellers are doing, and then saying, oh, this is really popular, we should make one of those. And so then they make one of those and then they promote it higher in their search results. And next thing you know, the other guy's out of business. And Amazon will tell you that's not supposed to happen. But when Bezos was asked about it today, he said he could not deny that it had happened. And he said the company was investigating, which it has been saying for months now.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: How did he do? How did Jeff Bezos do in his debut?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Look, he is a very genial presence. He, I would say, he, he did his best to come across as reasonable. And frankly, it's easy to come across as reasonable when you're being constantly interrupted, right? <Laughs> Sometimes I feel like Congress would be better off if they would just let these guys talk for a little while. Like, you might actually learn something, you know? You know, but I will say he did stumble. For example, one of the members of Congress said in relation to this problem of counterfeit goods, when people go to sell something on your Website…

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> LUCY MCBATH (D-GA): Do you require a real name and address? Yes or no?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I believe we do, but let, let me get back to your office…

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: ...And Bezos didn't know. And the member said...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Do you require a phone number? Yes or no?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: That seems like a fairly basic, fundamental question that you would assume the CEO of Amazon would know.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I don’t know if it’s required. I think we often have it.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And he did not know.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: So briefly then, how do you verify that each of these pieces of information is accurate?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Uh, I don’t know the answer to your question.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <Laughs>

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And that was useful for me to know.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Something refreshing to see during this hearing, which I certainly didn't see during the impeachment hearings, was it seemed like Democrats and Republicans were, like, united in purpose, if not motivation?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yeah, I think it's fair to say that both the Republicans and the Democrats are frustrated with these tech companies with almost an equal level of intensity. But I would also say that while there are only some of those complaints are are rooted in reality. Like, Republicans really only have one message, which is they believe that there is a conspiracy among tech companies to systematically disadvantage conservatives from using their platforms.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> REP. MATT GAETZ (R-FL): Mike Wacker came out and was a whistleblower indicating that the manual blacklist targets that Google specifically goes after are those who support President Trump, who hold a conservative viewpoint. And he left your company in 2019 because he was speaking out against these outrage mobs.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And that is despite the fact that a preponderance of evidence shows that conservative elected officials outperform Democratic elected officials when it comes to the sheer reach and engagement that the things that they post on those networks receive.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Does it seem like something might finally happen?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I think that, yes, something will happen. I think that we will see antitrust legislation against Google this summer. I think we'll probably see an antitrust case against Facebook, although probably not before the election. And of course, the results of the election could change that outcome.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: [SCORING IN - THE CHILLS]

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: People don't realize that there are now antitrust investigations being led separately by the Federal Trade Commission, the Department of Justice and multiple groupings of state attorneys general into Facebook, Amazon, Google and Apple. And so while I don't expect that the result, is that going to be every tech company, you know, broken up into smithereens? I do think we are going to see something meaningful come out of all of that. It just seems unimaginable that all of those investigations would turn out to be for naught.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Casey Newton’s got a very good newsletter called The Interface. You can sign up for it at the verge dot com slash interface. After the break, I’m going to talk to Kara Swisher about the staggering amount of power these  four dudes have.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: [MIDROLL]

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Something very strange happened on Fox News last week. Tucker Carlson went after Jeff Bezos for making 13 billion dollars in one day.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> TUCKER CARLSON: Now, 20 years ago. If that had happened, if a captain of industry had made 13 billion dollars in a single day while the country got poorer, the Democratic Party would have had something to say about it. Not anymore, because people getting rich are members of the Democratic Party.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: But that wasn’t particularly strange. It’s rare anyone makes 13 billion dollars in a day. It’s worth questioning how that happened. The strange part transpired at the end of Tucker’s show when he was doing his hand off with Sean Hannity who always follows. You’ve seen these handoffs on cable. They’re usually fluffy, you know, flattering, fatuous. This one was not that.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <CLIP> TUCKER CARLSON: Have a great night! And now Sean Hannity takes over from New York.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Alright, Tucker. People who make money, they provide goods and services. People want need and desire. That's America. It's called freedom, capitalism. And as long as it's honest, right? People decide. All right, Tucker, great show...

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: What you can’t see is Tucker’s face. He is frowning. He looks displeased with his colleague who called him out. It is rare to see Sean Hannity call out Tucker Carlson on live TV. And it was strange that the thing they were pecking at each other was the wealth of Jeff Bezos. Kara Swisher noticed as well and wrote about it for the New York Times.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Tucker Carlson looked totally tweaked. And then he had to sort of dial it back in a tweet saying well, if it was dishonestly, then obviously not. But honestly, I believe in capitalism. So it was this weird thing but the point of the matter is the $13 billion and everyone focused on the money that Jeff Bezos has, or the money Mark Zuckerberg has. All the tech moguls, Bloomberg keeps a list, have made enormous amounts of money during the pandemic.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: For people like Tucker Carlson, who can't really quite wrap their heads around how someone like Jeff Bezos could make 13 billion dollars…

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Right.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: … in one day, how does that happen?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: The stock of Amazon. Like he owns a lot of Amazon. And so Amazon's gone up. It's done a really good job of delivery. It's become a necessary service. We've sort of fast forwarded a decade in terms of use of delivery services. And he is the one who has the services that work in a pandemic really well compared to other retailers. Now, other retailers are trying really hard. But Amazon is like, you know, just doing great. And of course, they've got their cloud services, which has always been super strong. And he's, you know, sort of trying to virus-proof his distribution system. Not always successful. There's been a lot of illnesses at Amazon warehouses.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Has it borne out the same for Google and Facebook and Apple, too?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Everybody. All of them are doing great and they're more powerful ever as they go, you know, to try to get Congress not to legislate against them.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: How should people be thinking about it? I mean, is it great that these American tech companies are profiting hugely off of this pandemic? Or is it problematic? I mean, did they set up the businesses that would succeed in this moment? And should we be happy for them?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Well, it is what it is, right? As President Trump likes to say. You know, they do have these businesses—they're not in the restaurant business, they're not in the theater business. But everybody is being accelerated by a decade. That's what you have to think about. This is — things trending that were going in Amazon's direction or Google’s direction are now accelerated. And so, you know, Mark Cuban—I interviewed him yesterday on Pivot—and he was like, this is a huge economic experiment to see if we're going to actually change our economy, which we are. Our economy is about to change in a massive way in terms of workers, types of benefits, and lots of stuff like that. It's just it was trending that way, but now it's really trending that way.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: You seem to suggest in your op-ed in The New York Times that people should spend less time worrying about how much money these guys are making and spend more time thinking about how much power they're amassing.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yes. I think about it like the Rockefellers. Look, they stayed rich. And good thing, because the foundation gave away lots of money later. And same thing with these rich people. They're giving … Mark’s giving away money, Mackenzie Scott is giving away money. So they're going to stay rich. The issue is, like, the Rockefellers got out of power when they were started to be legislation, like the power that they held over society. But the fact is that that's not going down until Amazon goes down. And so the question is, how much power should these companies and how much, how many guardrails and regulations and ways to stop them from being totally dominant? And there are no rules for the Internet companies compared to Wall Street or chemical companies or car comp ... everybody else has regulations except Internet people. And then on the side, right? You see this damage being done, whether it's hate speech or addiction or this and that. It's all systemic to the fact that they have total power and we have no control as a society.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And we've talked to you about this with you before. ANd Casey thinks there might finally be some antitrust action this summer. I guess we’ll see. Why is it so hard to do for tech?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I don't know. I don't understand it because, of course, because Republicans, Democrats can't agree on something they absolutely should agree on. Depending on the company, now the problem is each of these companies have a different issue. Apple, it has to do with the App Store. And that could maybe be by rules and regulations, right? That doesn't have to break up Apple to do that. Amazon's got some issues around Marketplace and also selling things like I think the people who sell on the marketplace have good question to be worried about Amazon products being sold under. I bought an Amazon safe the other day because it was so much cheaper it was and it was the same safe.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Is it like an Amazon-branded safe?

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: Yes! It is! It’s an Amazon safe. And I'm sure he has my, the numbers

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: <laughs> I didn’t think you’d trust that safe, Kara.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text:
It was just — it was like so I tend to try to buy — and then I'm like, why am I buying branded stuff? They're only, I’m being charged for branded so why not like this white label stuff that Amazon makes? Batteries? Why should I pay triple for batteries because they're Duracell when they're the exact same batteries. And so, you know, you sort of sit there, you're like, which one which ridiculous conglomerate do I want to advantage, here? But the one who has lower prices. And so that's the issue with them. And then there's Google, which, of course, has search dominance. You've seen a lot of stories recently about that. They advantage their products in search. And besides the fact that they have so much search dominance, which is crazy, right? 

SEAN

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I wonder, you know, if the last few months have taught us anything, it's that, like, people still do have power in our democracy. But I feel like this is the sort of evergreen question we ask on our show, like, what would it take for people to rise up and say, ‘Hey, you know what, Facebook. You know what, Instagram, Twitter, you've gone too far. You need to do something about X.’ And I wonder, I still wonder what it would take to get people there.

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: I don't know. Because, you know, the problem is you get a lot of free good stuff that you like. You know, that's I always, as you know, I call citizens “cheap dates” to the tech companies. They get all the money we get, like a dating app or a map. “God, I got a map! Ahhh!” Like, “Thank you so much!” Like, what do you mean? You took data from the government that we paid for and then repurpose it and sold it to us and then took our data. And now you have 13 billion dollars in one day. Oh, how nice that is. And that said, like, these are innovative people have created really great products. They just need some regulation. By the way, welcome to your billions, Mr. Bezos. He created something from nothing, but he sat on the system that was created for him by the government. And the government should have some say in some of it. Like, and they shouldn't be able to sell a safe for half the price of another company and, and then put it up there in front of you and then being the only way it can be delivered. And then, you know, it takes just a second to be like, ‘Oh, I'm exhausted with COVID. My kids are screaming, I need a friggin safe. Like, just deliver it to me, Mr. Bezos.’

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR
text: And what if we do just give up and submit to Facebook and Amazon and Apple and Twitter. I mean—

episodeName: JULY 29, 2020 / TIM, MARK, JEFF, AND SUNDAR

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

episodeName: August 3, 2020 / Who’s Karen? And what’s BIPOC?

I think separating and actually having a term like BIPOC matters. Black and indigenous peoples, their existence in the United States is different, uniquely different compared to every other group that we've minoritized based in this country. How you get to a country has a long lasting impact on your continued existence in that country. So, for example, for Africans in America who were enslaved here, being brought to this country as enslaved people, being forcibly immigrated to a country, they did not come by choice, that the impact, the lasting impact on them from generation to generation. text: On Tuesday afternoon, I was driving home, passing by the port of Beirut, as I have done so many times before. There was a bit of traffic. So actually, the worse off you are as a country, the more money you're going to spend and borrowing money to get back because we don't trust you, because you have bad credit. So we're a country with bad credit emerging from a war with not much infrastructure. So to build that infrastructure, you had to accrue so much more debt. And that debt has been piling and piling and piling.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: And that debt crisis has led to a banking crisis?

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: So the banking crisis is linked to the debt crisis because the banks are the primary lender to the government. So when Lebanon emerged from the war, nobody wanted to lend Lebanon money. So Lebanon ended up taking a lot of money from local banks that charged really high interest rates because they didn't actually have faith in this government. So the government accumulated a lot of money; however, because the government wasn't really making money and because there wasn't really any industry in the country and people had no incentive to build any industry because the interest rates were so high in the bank, you know, so nothing was being built in the country. And all of that money was being spent by the government because the banks were again loaning money to the government for interest rates to make their own profits. So the banks did very well in Lebanon for a long time. But as the political crises, you know, mounted in the country, people started to get nervous about the banks’ ability to keep funding the government, but the government's ability to pay the banks back and the banks started to restrict the amount of money you can withdraw because people started running to the bank and trying to withdraw all of their money. And so that means that now we don't really have access to the money that we put in the bank, our deposits. We can only access a small allowance, which could be a few hundred bucks a month.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: And then I guess that brings us to the currency crisis.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: Yeah. Not only are you not able to get cash from the bank very easily in any any great amount, but the cash that you do get is worth, you know, 20 cents to the dollar. So if you had a dollar in your pocket, that's 20 cents you have now. If you had one hundred bucks, that's 20 bucks. So it's it's a massive blow to anyone. And that also applies to your salary, like whatever you make every month, you know, cut that down by 80 percent. Add to this that when you go to the store to buy groceries, everything is like doubled and tripled the price. So things like a bag of shredded cheese, you might, you know, buy to make a quesadilla or something, right? That used to cost, like, you know, six or seven bucks. And now it's the equivalent of like 20 or 30 dollars. All of these crises are inherently linked.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: How are people responding to this three-pronged crisis?

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: Well, people are really, really suffering. I mean, if your salary gets cut by 80 percent and the prices of goods go up, you kind of worry about how you're going to feed your children. So people have been selling items. There's been like some websites where people are selling like their household items, even dishes I've seen for sale or bartering. Crime has gone up. There was a viral video circulating in Lebanon of a guy who held up a pharmacy with a gun to buy diapers.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: I’ve never seen that. Let me look it up.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: Oh yeah, this is like the most passive robbery you can imagine. The guy is holding a gun but he seems pretty resigned. They’re putting the diapers in a bag and he’s slowly walking out.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: People are really suffering on a daily, just to just to get by, just to get a meal. About half of the country now is under the poverty level. And, of course, the Covid outbreak has definitely made everything worse because people can't get to their jobs. We've had a lot of lockdowns and we're going into another lockdown right now. There's lots of depression and there were some suicides related to the financial situation as well. So people are very anxious. They're very worried about their future, about their children. They're trying to escape this country as they have always done for decades. People have tried to escape Lebanon. And that's why you have so many Lebanese living abroad and immigrants and refugees. So yeah, it's definitely leading people to give up hope and it’s also much harder for the poorest segments of Lebanses society. Not only have the middle class become poor but the poor have become, you know, extremely impoverished.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: Late last year we covered the protests in Lebanon over this WhatsApp tax the government tried to impose. To some degree those protests were successful. The tax didn’t happen. The prime minister resigned. After everything that’s happened since, do people still have hope they can affect change in the country or are people giving up?

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: It's very difficult to dig yourself out of a deep hole. And I think it's also very difficult to reimagine a political system that has been in the making for decades. And a lot people rely on it and believe in it. And so the only, the only solution to Lebanon is for the IMF to loan Lebanon more money. And again, that means more debt. And, you know, and so that the best solution would be for Lebanon to start generating income, to start building industries. But it doesn't really have the infrastructure for that because, again, it's a war torn country. So another problem that Lebanon faces is that, you know, Lebanon decisions are not made only in Lebanon. The United States, you know, backs certain leaders in Lebanon. Iran backs certain groups in Lebanon, France, Saudi Arabia. They all have their favorite. So Lebanon is kind of like a an international chessboard where, you know, for decades now, different countries have tried to support different sides. And so I think in some ways, Lebanon is like a country that's unfinished. It's not really formed yet. And that formation of any country, I think, revolves around one side winning, one side emerging victorious to lead a country, usually at a great cost of violence. Well, we've had all the violence in Lebanon, but nobody won. So Lebanon is a country of no winners and no losers, which is kind of democratic because everybody gets a say or a lot of political parties get a say, but nothing really gets done in the country. So it's really hard to imagine a way out of it other than getting more debt to try to restructure the debt. You know, for the umpteenth time and passing on this debt to the next generation, although people are not really weren't willing to lend Lebanon money either because they've seen so much money in the country disappear. So it's a real tragedy, I think, for the people who live here, who just wake up everyday and that's where they are. I mean, they didn't decide, you know, on lending rates. They didn't decide on taking out those loans. They just average people who are now suffering under the worst economic crisis. So we could see violence you know, And at the same time, there is violence on our border. There is you know ongoing confrontation between Hezbollah and Israel. And that's been going on for years, that could flare up anytime. You know, that has flared up in the past and to create wars that have set the country back further.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
text: I think that people are trying to be creative. They're trying to start out small industries, to try to go back to farming. You know, Lebanon, is the country, the Middle East that has, you know, rivers and valleys and greenery around us or a lot of deserts, you know. And so it's a very fertile, fertile crescent is where farming started thousands of years ago. It's a beautiful country for tourism. You know, it's a gorgeous country for history. Every part of the world has been here. You've got Roman temples that look better than the ones in Rome preserved. And my heart goes out to people that are really at the margin of society right now because they're really suffering badly. And, you know, I would just say if people who want to help out, you know, they can visit the country, they could try to help people out here because, again, it's a great country. It's a hidden gem. Unfortunately, politically, it's not been able to get a break and a rest from the powers that be, whether they're local or foreign.

And, if anything I guess, one positive outlook of this is that the world is paying attention right now. So I hope, I hope good things come of that.

episodeName: August 5, 2020 / What’s going on in Lebanon
