episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: [THEME]

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: My great great grandmother, Esther, grew up in Eastern Europe and spent the later years of her life in South Philadelphia.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: She naturalized at the immigration station on Washington Avenue, which was kind of like Philadelphia's Ellis Island point of entry for mostly Eastern European immigrants at the turn of the 20th century. She settled a few blocks away with her family.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: In 1918, my great great grandmother Esther died. She died in the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic and died in the midst of caring for family. I, I knew some of the details, but it really kind of floated through family lore. There wasn't a big reference point, not just in our own family, but in our culture about what that pandemic meant for life in the city. So, you know, at the onset of our pandemic, I had a conversation with organizers of an exhibition here in Philadelphia, the Mutter Museum, who had opened an exhibition a year before our most recent pandemic about the thousands of lives lost in Philadelphia in the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: They had pulled death certificates from anyone who had died of influenza or related causes. And it was in conversation with one of their curators that they presented me with this record of my great great grandmother. It says she passed away in October of 1918 of pneumonia that was onset from influenza. It lists her family members. It lists where she was buried. What I was gathering about the past and my family was that a group of at that point, fairly recent Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe living in South Philadelphia, were caring for themselves and their neighbors in a city that didn't have the big picture plans to deal with the public health crisis, especially in vulnerable communities. So it felt uncanny to that moment of discovery and the current pandemic we're in to see that the story of a public health crisis that really falls upon vulnerable residents to care for themselves and their neighbors. It uh, <laughs> it felt uncanny.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Paul Farber is a historian and director of the Monument Lab -- it’s a public art and history studio based in Philadelphia. Until Covid-19, the 1918 pandemic was kind of a historical footnote for Americans. There are no national monuments, no statues in front of federal buildings, no vast parks calling us to remember it. Today on the show, we're going to talk about why. And why we should think about commemorating Covid-19 differently.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: More than 675,000 Americans died of influenza in the 1918 pandemic. I've read in places that if you judge that based on the population today, it'd be the equivalent of over 2 million Americans dying. You know, something that kind of haunts us in this moment, you know, approximately the same number of soldiers died in World War One of flu complications as they did in battle. There are hundreds, if not thousands of World War One monuments and markers and other forms of popular remembrance that aren't just in bronze and marble

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: So the memorials we do have -- to conflicts like World War I -- what impact do they have on the public?

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: In different communities, in different time periods, there's a kind of all kinds of other imperatives that inform. For example, you may have seen war memorials that list out the names of individual soldiers or medics who from a given community lost their lives. And if you live in a small town, even if it's several dozen names, it, it registers because you may recognize the last name or understand them in the context of a family. In other cases, there's the incorporation actually of artillery or cannons or other kinds of instruments of war. But you generally, what you would see is kind of the transfer of the experience of war and that sense of loss transformed into something else. And it's meant to be a place of remembrance, of healing. But far too often, they're hard to upkeep. They, they are the very form kind of invites being still and frozen in time and the end of a sentence, so to speak, rather than a place of continuation and bridge forward. I mean, there is another...you know, after World War II, you would see an expansion of the kind of living memorial veterans parks, veterans highways, veteran's stadiums. The idea that veterans wanted life to go on as well.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: It seems like memorials have a lot of controversy just baked into them because they sort of take a position on who was a force of good or who was the force of bad or who deserves to be remembered.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Absolutely. Those with more power, those with more money, those with more time build monuments that are important to them. But we also know that if you don't have the time, the money, the official power, you gather next to monuments that exist or you build your own. And so I think what's important as we...look, as we...if you walk around your neighborhood or your town, I would imagine you're already seeing Covid memorials and some kind of way. It might be a candle lit in a windowsill. It might be a sign for front line workers or sanitation workers on someone's lawn. We're already seeing it because we're already doing it. One of the ways that we cope and survive and move forward is by grieving and making space for mourning and understanding that that's part of our everyday condition. The pandemic, you know, some people called as “the great equalizer” and I think instead, you know, it's a great revealer of existing fault lines, the deep socioeconomic and racial disparities in mortality and health care, the systemic racism that put Black Americans at at great risk, disproportionately facing higher casualty counts. The deep seated anti-Asian racism that we're seeing now. The effect on women and their labor, these are all part of this pandemic. So if we try to boil down public memory to the heroes and the foes we're only going to superficially numb this collective pain and we're going to fail to be able to address those fault lines that existed before Covid. You know, this is an opportunity that we have to meet to be able to do better, so that we can really do the work of recovery.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: If there was a memorial for the 1918 flu, what do you think it would have done for your great grandmother's family or her descendants?

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Well, I would hope that there would have been many kinds of memorials. Some of them could be as big as a city block and represent, you know, in this case, just how impactful the 1918 flu pandemic was on the city of Philadelphia. And really give us a sense of the groups of immigrants and African-American migrants and workers who were deeply impacted and didn't always have a chance to get out of their immediate neighborhoods or had to do great work if they did survive to care for their friends, loved ones and neighbors. So I'd want to see that on a citywide level. But I think on the more neighborhood, street by street, family by family, an understanding of what life was like in that moment.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: That's the information I wish we knew more about because it really would have informed how we could have gone about our early days of the pandemic now.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Paul Farber is the director of the Monument Lab in Philadelphia. Coming up, we may not have a national monument yet, but people are still finding ways to remember Covid-19.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Alissa Wilkinson, you’re a film critic and culture reporter at Vox. And you recently wrote about memorials and people who lost loved ones to Covid. As more and more Americans get vaccinated, how are these people thinking about moving forward -- while also remembering those that passed away?

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: Yeah, there's a big tension between those two things. Part of it is that grief is delayed. So if you lost someone and then you had a socially distant Thanksgiving that didn't really feel like Thanksgiving, then the first Thanksgiving where their seat is empty is still in front of you, which means that we’ll be experiencing some of this loss and grief for a much longer period than we might have. The effects are going to be different. And as much as everyone wants to move on from this and, you know, everyone's been affected, whether or not they've lost someone, you know, do you want to move on if you're afraid that people are going to forget your loved one? And one big reason this could happen is that so many people have died that the individuals risk becoming just kind of one in a group. So there's some kind of need to bring the past into the present and preserve it for the future. And I think that's what a lot of people are grappling with. On the other hand, you know, I talked to a woman named Lisa who lost her father, who was living in an assisted living facility. She said she's, she's tired of death and wants to celebrate life. And that's a refrain that you hear a lot from people who are grieving as well.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: How have other memorials struck that balance between moving forward and remembering the past...which might still make them really sad or really angry?

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: The tendency, especially I think for Americans, is to try and put it in the past behind us to not remember the failures that brought us to this place. So we have a lot of accountability that we need to find in these memorials. There are some examples of that in the country. I think one notable example is in Montgomery, Alabama, a few years ago, the Equal Justice Initiative opened a memorial called the National Memorial for Peace and Justice. It's on six acres and it draws a line from slavery through lynching and racial terror to, you know, Black people who suffered humiliation during Jim Crow and all the way to racially-based police violence.

text: ...and I think Covid in some ways is the same in that there's a lot of dark truths about us that have been exposed during this time about how we deal with each other, about how we deal with limits on our freedom, preparedness of our government, all these different things we might wish they were in the past. episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: So a lot of what we've seen has been made by artists and arts organizations. There's a, there's an artist, Divya Mehra, who had a show in L.A. where it was just...it was two giant emojis, huge inflatable emojis of a wave and an urn.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial
text: So one thing that's come up a lot is that memorials of the future to Covid-19 victims, and just to this time, need to be solid and physical.

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial

episodeName: March 19, 2021 / Why America needs a national pandemic memorial

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?

So we know that roughly 34 million people in the U.S. smoke cigarettes and of those, somewhere between 35 and 40 percent of people are menthol users. So that would track out to maybe about 10 million people who smoke menthols, which is not an insignificant amount. Also, cigarette use has been steadily going down for the past two decades or so as more information has come out about health risks as the FDA started regulating it. But menthol use has tracked slower than overall declines in tobacco.

SEAN

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And so do we have any idea of how many of these roughly 10 million menthol smokers in the United States are black?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Eighty-five percent of Black smokers prefer menthol. So it's a vast majority of those users and those come from CDC figures.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: <CHAPELLE’S SHOW CLIP> DAVE CHAPELLE: Give it up for my new game show.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: I! KNOW! BLACK PEOPLE!

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Why do Black people love menthols so much?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: I don't, I don't know.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: That is correct. Nobody knows, nobody knows, for sure.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Well, there's been a long history starting from when menthols became popular in the first place of tobacco companies, specifically targeting Black communities through advertisements, through sponsorships of things like the Kool Jazz Festival.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: <CLIP> KOOL JAZZ FESTIVAL:  The 1982 Kool Jazz Festival. It's live, it’s hot, it's cool and it's coming.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: These like creative campaigns they would do where they literally would have vans going around in black communities and giving free samples.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text:
<CLIP> “EVERYDAY STRUGGLE” - NOTORIOUS BIG 

SARAH: A lot of those things have been discontinued since we've had more regulation of cigarettes. Like, for instance, they can't be doing billboards anymore. They can't be doing the magazine ads that they were doing in, in things like Essence and Ebony and Jet. So those things are discontinued. But one thing that is absolutely still going on is point-of-sale focus. So we know from data that the campaign for Tobacco Free Kids has collected that there are still disproportionately more tobacco retailers in Black communities than in other communities, and that there even are sometimes cheaper prices for menthols and for cigarillos. These cheap flavored cigars, which are a part of this conversation, too.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: <CLIP> CAMPAIGN FOR TOBACCO FREE KIDS: Menthol cigarettes are cheaper in Black neighborhoods. Big tobacco targets us because they think we're just easy money. They get cash. We get killed.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And so there is an intentional focus on getting black Americans, Black teens to focus on buying these products and making them more appealing to them.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And is a popularity among Black smokers in particular the reason there's legislation around this right now?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Yes. And it's also the reason why this has become a very charged conversation.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: <CLIP> NAACP’S JONATHAN BUTLER: The tobacco industry has perniciously targeted African-Americans with mentholated products, and thus the NAACP is in support of efforts to restrict the sale of menthol cigarettes and other flavored tobacco products because it impacts our African-American community.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: So you have members of the Congressional Black Caucus being divided over what this means. I spoke to Representative Al Lawson from Florida last year before this vote about what his experience was, and he talked about how when he was young, he remembered kids being let out of school early to pick tobacco in fields and how his father died from smoking related cancer. And he said this needs to be over for Black Americans. But then I would talk to someone like Yvette Clark from New York who would say, in my mind's eye, I see Eric Garner saying “I can't breathe,” because he died in a police headlock over selling cigarettes.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: <CLIP> REP. YVETTE CLARK: I cannot support H.R. 23 39 due to the potential dire consequences that would create additional stop and frisk opportunities of African-Americans and the constituents I took an oath to protect. I really believe that this is a health imperative. And if that is the case, the ban should be on all tobacco products and would be the best answer. But unfortunately, this bill does not do that. I yield back.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: So these are the two sides of the conversation, it's really personal and there's a lot of concern that if this legislation were to go into effect, it would give another reason for police to target black communities and for police brutality to continue.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Hmm. I think a lot of people understand the sort of motivations when it comes to personal health here or the health of our communities, but tell me more about the sort of policing angle here. How would this ban work? Does it stop the manufacture of menthols or the sale or or does it sort of criminalize the consumption? What exactly is it?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: So that's the really important part of it that advocates say means that it wouldn't lead to over-policing. It does not criminalize the consumption of these cigarettes. It criminalizes the sale of them. Of course, in practice, that will become difficult because states can always add on to existing legislation about tobacco. So if we pass a nationwide menthol ban is not necessarily something saying that states can't criminalize the possession and use of menthol cigarettes. They could do that, too.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: How are lawmakers responding to this argument that this could lead to more policing of Black Americans, especially?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text:
Many of them are saying that that argument is coming from the tobacco industry itself.

SEAN

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: You brought up tobacco companies, which dump a ton of money into the coffers of lawmakers in Washington. How are they responding? I assume they would prefer Washignton didn’t ban menthols?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Yeah, they're not thrilled. They have been targeting states and localities who have already passed menthol bans. They've been suing for them to drop those or introducing ballot measures to go against those. They've been arguing that this infringes on people's personal rights to smoke the tobacco that they want and that also this is an overreaction to parents' concerns about their children getting hooked on vapes and on tobacco products. And so their whole argument is we’ll just improve their sales and marketing so that children don't get their hands on the products and that that's the real issue, not menthol.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: If there was interest from the Biden administration to do something about this do they need Congress? Could this be something that the FDA just did on its own?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Yeah, funnily enough, they don't need Congress to do this. The Food and Drug Administration.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text:
Huh!

SARAH

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And like former smoker, to former smoker, I mean, if it did happen, it would kind of be a big deal for, like, the smoking community, which is an actual community, right?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Yeah, it would. I mean, it really, really would. We're talking, again, about at least 10 million people. We're talking about something that, you know, a lot of us got hooked on when we started smoking.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And what are people going to have to do if this goes through? They're going to have to, like, chew minty gum and smoke cigarettes at the same time, huh?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text:
<laugh> I could see it. Do you remember those those ones where you'd crush the little menthol thing.

SEAN

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: More on the menthols in a minute.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: [MIDROLL]

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: The federal government is considering a ban on menthols but a few states have already taken action. Massachusetts banned flavored tobacco. And California’s considering it too.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Jody Armour is a law professor at the University of Southern California who thinks it’s a terrible idea.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: I opposed the bill, for one thing, because I saw it as an effort to revisit the failed logic of the war on drugs, the logic of prohibition, you can't really oppose the logic of prohibition on the one hand, which we have been doing, especially for the last five to 10 years in the name of decarceration, and then, on the other hand, turn around and enthusiastically embrace that same logic in the name, again, of anti-racism and protecting Black lives. And so the legislation and a lot of these bans suggest that the way to protect Black lives is to keep Black people from being able to consume products on the same footing as White folks.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: I think your perspective on this might be surprising to some people, because as we established in the first half of the show, this legislation is meant to protect Black lives. Menthol cigarettes and flavored tobacco have been marketed more effectively, perhaps to Black Americans for, for decades. And now we've got Black teenagers smoking potentially more flavored tobacco. And so you see this, though, as something that could harm Black lives. How come?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Frankly, the road to hell is paved with good intentions and coercive benevolence.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: That's what we learned from the War on Drugs. We learn that, you know, laws that invite therapeutic policing, if you will, you know, paternalistically protecting people from their own desires and preferences and wants and not respecting their agency to make choices that we might even consider unhealthy. But we view it also as very unhealthy to have any kind of carceral intervention to try to address a health problem. If we think we have a health problem with cigarettes, then we should have health-based solutions and not solutions that are rooted in the police and in jails and in bans and in illicit markets that bans give rise to and, you know, Eric Garner is almost a poster person for the negative consequences that can flow from efforts to regulate, overregulate cigarettes or ban cigarettes. You know, he was selling loosies on the sidewalk because there wasn't a ready availability at a certain price point for cigarettes by many of the consuming public. Now, you ban menthol altogether, and it's going to be even more of a strong temptation for an illicit market to develop. And the temptations to participate in that market are going to be very great among Black youth and Black folk who are already economically challenged often and seeking any way to bring in a little extra income, including through an illicit market mechanism.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: OK, it sounds like you're making two arguments now, professor, and I want to talk about each of them individually, it sounds like.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: You're making this sort of live free or die argument about policing people's health choices. And then it also sounds like you're talking about the actual police. You brought up Eric Garner and how this whole chokehold business that led to his death actually arose from him selling loosie cigarettes in Staten Island that day. Let's talk about that first. Congresswoman Karen Bass said the federal bill that would stop people from selling flavored tobacco would stop them from just selling it, not possessing it. How would it still contribute to mass incarceration?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Yeah, well, that's a canard that the bill only addresses the sale of menthol cigarettes and not the use, you know, prohibition. Alcohol prohibition in this country, the 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act, they just prohibited the sale of alcohol. But we saw the kind of calamity that that turned into anyway. And so, the whole logic of incarceration also requires the police to start their crackdown on the sellers, right?  We're not going after the users, but the sellers like the Eric Garner, we are going to be able to go after police say, in the name of protecting the Black community.  And the Black Lives Matter movement, when the streets were roiling over the summer with protest, pastors and activists, what they were asking for is a non-carceral approach to our social problems, a health based approach that doesn't rely on bans and criminalization and law enforcement to address our social issues.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: And this brings us back to the health argument that I wanted to ask you more about. It sounds like you're saying we don't need the government to tell us what we should smoke and what we shouldn't smoke or or what flavor of tobacco we should smoke and shouldn't smoke. I mean, how far do you take that argument? Do you take it closer to what Oregon recently did in the last election where they decriminalized all drugs?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: You can't talk out of both sides of your mouth. You can't oppose the logic of prohibition in the name of decarceration and anti-racism, right, when it comes to weed and other drugs, and then turn around and enthusiastically embrace that same logic of prohibition in illicit markets that flow from it in the name of anti-racism and protecting Black lives. You have to be consistent in your opposition to the logic of prohibition when it comes to weed, when it comes to alcohol, when it comes to cigarettes, when it comes to all kinds of contraband that adults may want to make choices about the consumption of. And you certainly shouldn't say that we're going to police Black vice differently than White vice because that's what this winds up doing. This is a ban on a brand of cigarettes that 85 percent of blacks use. Right? We're going to deny you a product that we are allowing your white counterparts to get to in pretty much the same form. You know, we can quibble about whether menthol really is makes the product a little more dangerous, a little more carcinogenic or habit-forming perhaps at the margins, but not enough to justify, again, embracing the logic, failed logic of prohibition.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: Professor, can I ask you, are you a menthol smoker?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: No! I don't smoke at all. And I discourage smoking. You know, I discourage my three sons. I tell everybody I can talk to, do not smoke, don't smoke menthol, don't smoke non-menthol, you know, it’s bad for your health. But I want to take those kinds of approaches. I want to appeal to people as adults who can make decisions and not impose my preferences on them. Right. And we've made great strides in this country in reducing the use of cigarettes. The percentage of Americans who smoke now is a fraction of what it was in the mid 60s at the height of smoking. And we got those deep cuts in the use of cigarettes by Americans, not by criminalizing tobacco. We came up with non-carceral ways, educational ways and other ways to reduce tobacco consumption without falling back on our collective addiction to criminality and crime.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: That being said, do you realize that your opposition to this legislation, unfortunately or fortunately, depending on your perspective, puts you in league with the tobacco industry? That if someone who works for Camel or Marlboro hears you making this argument right now, they'll be really happy to hear it?

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: The tobacco companies right now are on the right side of the issue. They're on the right side of history. They may not be on the right side and are not on the right side of history when it comes to promoting healthful outcomes. In the 50s, 40s, 60s, when they were advertising that cigarettes were not harmful. That was the kind of fraud that they should have had to reckon for and reckon with. And, you know, there have been suits and there has been some reckoning. But now we're talking about cases in which, like alcohol, people are told up front that there are risks that accompany this particular activity. And now you as adults, we're going to respect your, your ability to make choices.

episodeName: 25 March 2021 / The end of minty cigarettes?
text: What a lot of the people who put Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in office were saying, many of those people were the ones marching in the streets throughout the summer, what many of them were saying was there is no social or health problem for which the answer is more police. Right? So hopefully once you start with that message, the hope is you can come up with other solutions, other non-carceral alternative interventions. But among those solutions should not be the more police, more prohibition, more illicit markets, more Eric Garners.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: A while ago, producer Gabrielle Berbey cold-called a church in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in search of the origin story of an argument we’re all having right now.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Synthesizer music plays, persistent, evocative of a journey through time and space.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: We are in the midst of the most ambitious vaccine rollout the world has ever seen. There’s finally hope that all of this will end. But this hope depends almost entirely on how many people will be willing to get the vaccine. There’s still real fear around what this vaccine will do to us. And this battle between hope and fear? It’s not the first time we’ve seen it in this country. It started in this church, a hundred years ago … .

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Music out, suddenly.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Thank you for talking to me. This is, like, such a random call. (Laughs.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: … Where the current pastor picked up the phone.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The strains of a distorted organ musicsong play in the background.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Are you in the church now?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Oh, I can hear that. Yeah.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The original pastor of this church was a guy named Henning Jacobson, who took a personal—and very public—stand over vaccination in 1902.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: What are you seeing right now?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: He looks like a, uh … He’s got, like, wild hair and a wild beard kind of. I think he was, like, kind of like a fire-and-brimstone sort of preacher.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: He’s dignified, I would say. Dignified.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Sort of asking, “What are you going to do with me?” [Berbey laughs.] And I’m like, “I don’t know, Henning. I don’t know, man.”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (A long beat of organ music with no speech.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I mean, it’s almost a little bit unfortunate that, like, the thing that … You Google his name, the first thing that pops up is Henning Jacobson v. The State of Massachusetts, which is, like, you know … [Chuckles.] In some sense, I suppose he was the first anti-vaxxer.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music changes tone dramatically, becoming airy, meditative, and light.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: This week, the story of a man who took a stand for something he believed in … and asked the Supreme Court to step into an argument that we still haven’t settled, over where the line is between our rights over our bodies and our duty to others.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I’m Julia Longoria. This is The Experiment, a show about our unfinished country.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The story of the Henning Jacobsons case has this weird quality about it where people keep reaching back to try and find some kind of meaning from the life of this one anti-vax pastor.

text: (Classical music begins to play, light and lush, starting with strings before a clarinet melody enters in.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: So, if we were gonna do the movie in your head of how Henning’s life went, how does it start?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Let’s see. With the little knowledge I have, I have to figure out a movie. The movie would have to start in Sweden.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music becomes lively and energetic.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The movie would start in Henning’s boyhood in 19th-century rural Sweden, in a town called Yllestad, which is a remote community settled near a big blue lake surrounded by rolling plains.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: If you wanted to focus the movie on what he is most famous or infamous for—which is the Supreme Court case—then a Hollywood movie would probably start with him sweating and in pain/having his first bad experience of the vaccine.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Henning first got vaccinated in Sweden when he was six years old.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And then he carries that memory into his later life.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And then I imagined him coming to this country, wide-eyed, 13 years old, and sort of being struck by the diversity of America.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Another strong beat of music.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Then he ends up going to college and seminary. All I know about them is from the few records we have here at church. It’s really not much to go on. You know, you should really talk to a historian. (Laughs.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music plays up, and then cuts out with a record scratch.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Can you introduce yourself?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Sure. I’m Michael Willrich, I’m a chair of the History Department at Brandeis University, and I’m the author of Pox

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Professor Willrich has his own version of the Henning Jacobson biopic.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (More classical music plays, though more sparse this time, and a little more distant.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I would open with him going down to the docks in Boston.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: A grown Henning Jacobson would take frequent trips from his home in Cambridge down to the city of Boston.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Waiting as immigrant ships came into the harbor, meeting the Swedish immigrants who came off those ships, and finding jobs and housing for them, and basically being a kind of working-class minister.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: He just worked on building this community of people from scratch, gathering people together.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Pastor Lutjohann calls him a sort of community organizer.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: He founded a church—an immigrant church—here, among people who were—for the most part—poor laborers who came to this country not with a lot of money seeking economic opportunity.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The classical music changes to become a heavy, somber bell chime.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: 1901, there’s a smallpox outbreak in the northeast of this country.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Smallpox was one of the most deadly diseases the world had ever seen at that point. It would result in fevers and oozing sores that would sometimes cover people’s entire face and body.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: It was the same disease that European settlers brought to North America in the 17th century, when it killed Native American populations—many, many people. 200 years later, there were still outbreaks in major U.S. cities. And, in 1901, Cambridge was in the middle of one of those outbreaks.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: It was part of this wave of epidemics across the nation.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: So the city of Cambridge decided to make vaccination mandatory.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: They’re very diligent about it. They go door-to-door.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And I guess Jacobson was sufficiently prominent, because of his role as a minister in the community, that the chairman of the local board of health came to his door and knocked on his door and, you know, offered-slash-asked-slash-demanded [Chuckled.] that he be vaccinated, and Jacobson refused.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: He refuses, because he believed that it was his right to refuse vaccination. He’s like, “Nobody can tell me what to put in my body.” Part of the reason for that was that he had had some adverse side effects taking vaccines previously. And I think his son did, as well. And so I imagine he was probably scared by that experience and he didn’t want to live through it again.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Was there good reason for people to be scared or skeptical of vaccines?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: There was pretty good reason. Public health departments would send out teams of vaccinators—very often in the middle of the night—into tenement districts, uh, usually inhabited by, you know, immigrant, working-class people. They go door-to-door on these sort of vaccine raids, and they’d  inspect the arms of everyone who lived in these homes to see that they had been recently vaccinated—that they had a kind of vaccine scar on their upper arms. In his own community of Cambridge, people are jumping out of windows and running the other way, or are getting doctors to sign phony vaccination certificates. I found one episode in the historical record from Kentucky, where the vaccinators went into an African-American neighborhood of this community, and, uh, ordered everybody to get vaccinated, and those who refused were handcuffed and vaccinated at gunpoint.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Quietly.) Wow.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: There was outright violence used to compel people to be vaccinated, and Jacobson certainly would have been aware of that.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Lightly.) I mean, call me an anti-vaxxer, but that sounds really extreme.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: It’s the very extreme edge of this.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Though most Americans did accept vaccines at the time, this kind of forcible vaccination was part of the reason there was a healthy transatlantic anti-vaccination movement already in motion.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Every local community of any significant size might have an anti-vaccination league or society. Typically they’d form during an epidemic or during some period when compulsion was on the rise. They’d meet in small meeting places. They would publish leaflets, uh, that they’d circulate on the city streets.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Jacobson attended at least one anti-vax meeting, but he wasn’t officially part of the movement. All he did was, for himself, refuse to get vaccinated.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: This sort of set this chain of events in motion in which he ended up being brought before a local criminal court. Uh, and the charge was “the crime of refusing vaccination.”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And, eventually, a team of lawyers took on Jacobson’s case and fought it in court.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The question of the case was whether Jacobson could be fined $5 for refusing to be vaccinated.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: To help us understand Jacobson

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: One of my strange pandemic outings over the summer was in search of the graveyard of one of Jacobson’s lawyers.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: She lives in Boston, where she’s the Director of Northeastern’s Center for Health Policy and Law.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I think I found what is his tombstone only a few miles away from my house.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Surprised.) Really?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And I went “Wow!” And then went, you know, “Nobody else knows what the hell I’m doing.” (All laugh heartily.) But it was something to do on a pandemic Saturday, right?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: She is completely obsessed with this case. Like, dedicated much of her career to understanding it.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Jacobson, to me, is this incredibly rich case. It is so Delphic.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (A heavy, echoey, infrequent sound plays in the background.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Delphic, like—as in, like, a Greek Oracle?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Yeah, in the sense that different people read it differently because you can see in it what you want to see in it. And I think, as with many texts, we bring our own worldviews into what we see in Jacobson.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music becomes more elaborate, percussive.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: You can see this in the arguments that Jacobson’s lawyers made. They were all over the map, laying out almost, like, a menu of options for why someone might object to a vaccine.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: They sort of threw the whole constitutional kitchen sink at this case. They argued that vaccination was dangerous, that compulsion was unnecessary, that this was a violation of every individual’s right to make choices about their own bodies.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Religious ideas also made their way into some of their arguments.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Music out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: There’s a lot of religious terminology in the briefs. I don’t have the exact quote up. Um, my computer went to bed. Can I—can you give me one second to wake up my computer?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Yeah, of course.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Music back in.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Searchingly, stretching out each syllable before “Okay.”) And I will find it. Okay. So this is from the brief before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, filed on behalf of Jacobson, asked, quote, “Can the free citizen of Massachusetts, who is not yet a pagan nor an idolater, be compelled to undergo this rise and to participate in this new—no, revived form of worship of the sacred cow?”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: As in, vaccines are a worship of the sacred cow?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Well, there was this view … The word vaccine itself is from the Latin for “cow.”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The word “vaccine” comes from vacca, or cow. Cows were a key part of the first vaccines ever made for smallpox.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: A country doctor might keep a cow on hand for the purpose of producing vaccine.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Scientists found that people who were exposed to cowpox from cows had immunity to smallpox.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Smallpox vaccine, as material, was live viruses taken from, uh, oozing sores on the bellies of calves.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Vaccines and their precursors injected the material from boils.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music slowly fades out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: … The pus … And put it under the skin of somebody who had not had smallpox. [A beat.] I’m probably telling you more than you want to know.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: That just, like, opened up a new room in my brain. I had no idea that it …

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And you can find similar language in contemporary anti-vaccinationist websites. “It’s pagan. You’re putting something of the cow in you. You’re worshiping the cow in the revering of vaccination.”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Wow.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: This fear and anger towards vaccination goes way back. This sense that it is somehow unnatural and ungodly goes way back.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: These are the arguments that Jacobson’s lawyers made to a judge. But the court struck all those arguments down. Jacobson lost his case at the local level—and then his lawyers appealed all the way to the Supreme Court.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (A wispy, ethereal music begins to play underneath the dialogue.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Jacobson is the first case where the Supreme Court took a claim of sovereignty over one’s body in terms of medical treatment seriously.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: This was one of the first times the Court was presented with this big question

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The Court held that he could be.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The Supreme Court said, “Yes, Jacobson. You have to pay the fine.”

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The Court’s decision was—was really pretty interesting.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Historian Michael Willrich again.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Music out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The opinion of the court was written by Justice John Marshall Harlan, who was a Civil War veteran. And for him, it was clear that this case was a legitimate exercise of the police power of the state. Smallpox was extremely dangerous and he insisted that, by the same logic that a government can raise an army to prevent a military invasion and can compel individual citizens to, uh, take up arms and risk being shot down in the defense of their country—by that same sort of rationale, the government can fight off a deadly disease and demand individuals to be vaccinated, even if it violated their sense of personal liberty or conscience or whatever.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: When there is a virus or some other disease coming in, personal liberty has to take a backseat to public safety.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Pastor Robin Lutjohann again.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And this is a sticky and tricky thing to argue and to try to get right. And it turns out that he was on the losing side of history there.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Soft, solemn piano music plays.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Since 1900, an estimated 300 million people in the world have died from smallpox. It was because of these mass vaccination campaigns that the very last known natural case of smallpox was recorded in 1977. It’s the first human disease to have been completely eradicated from the planet because of vaccines.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: There was this very short period—this wisp of history where humanity thought we had conquered infection.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: After the smallpox outbreak that Jacobson lived through—and the influenza pandemic of 1918—there weren’t very many large epidemics in the U.S. until 60 years later, when we started to battle AIDS.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: We just sort of assumed that contagion was only the stuff of horror films and movies. It was behind us.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Once you recognize contagion’s ubiquity, you realize that so much of human history has been forged by battles over contagion. Contagion and epidemics have brought out the best in humanity and the worst in humanity. Contagions have been the excuse for so many atrocities in the world and so much discrimination. You know, uh, witches were—you know, plague came and Jews were killed and witches were burned. And, we see this throughout history.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And so it’s a very delicate balance.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Contagion brings out fear in all of us. In the times we’re living right now, it’s not hard to get inside of Henning Jacobson’s head when he refused the vaccine. He did it because he was scared.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The piano music quietly slips off and ends.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I think I mentioned Henning Jacobson and his legacy in my sermon.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Pastor Lutjohann has thought a lot about Jacobson’s fear. At the very beginning of coronavirus, when everything was just starting to shut down, he thought about what to say to his congregation. He didn’t want them to be afraid. And so he preached about a story in the Bible that he thought could help.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: It was about how, like, there are these poisonous snakes.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: In the book of Numbers, God sent down a plague of poisonous snakes on the people of Israel.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The disobedient people of God wandering through the desert are punished by God.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And Moses—who was chosen by God to lead these people through the desert—watched as deadly snakes killed them, one by one. They were dying in droves, and people were terrified.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And then Moses does this strange thing where he has a bronze snake made, and he puts it up on a pillar and he displays it in front of everyone. And everybody who looks at the bronze snake on the pillar gets healed. So that’s the story.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Okay.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: And there’s a number of different ways to interpret that.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Yeah! I’m like, “What’s the message of that?” (Laughs.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: “What’s the message?” Right?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Lush, atmospheric electronic lounge music plays.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: The healing is going to come from the poison itself. How do the people bitten by the snake get healed? By looking at an image of the very snake.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I also mentioned to the congregation, you know, it’s also reminiscent of a very famous image that we see so often in medical sciences, which is also a serpent around the staff.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Right.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: This idea that somehow the deadly poison of the snake is also a way to unlock the possibility of healing. And it’s come true in modern vaccinations!

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Most of the way we get modern vaccinations is by somehow altering the disease itself and, ironically, injecting the disease into a human being.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: I mentioned Henning and I said, “Look, this is not just true about medicine. This is true about a lot of our lives, you know? Do you want to overcome your deepest fears and your most profound hang-ups? Well, often it is by actually going to the root of where they come from and facing up to them, rather than running away from them.” You know, you can’t keep running away. You got to go back to where the disease started, and that’s where the key is.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Jacobson’s case paved the way for governments to require vaccination for kids in schools. It’s been cited in New York and California recently to strike down people’s religious objections to vaccines.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Pastor Lutjohann is glad that Jacobson lost the case—even if it means he’s not sure where to put up that portrait of Jacobson in his church.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Music fades out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: We can be grateful for his work here.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Yeah.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: At the same time, also saying the dude was terribly mistaken—

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Yeah.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: —about this—this one thing for which unfortunately he’s most famous now. And I think, in a way, maybe that’s beautiful, because it then means that we don’t get to make an idol of him. We don’t get to make this perfect, pristine founding father of him. You know, he was complicated!

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Fluttering, flitting electric guitar chords play.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Henning Jacobson was complicated. And so is the legacy of his case. 20 years after his case was decided, the government used the same argument that it used against Jacobson to make one of the darkest, most infamous decisions in U.S. history.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Have you heard of Buck v. Bell?

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: No. [A beat.] Tell me about it!

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: That, after the break.

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (The music plays, quiets, then goes out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Midroll.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: (Symphonic electronic music plays, then fades out.)

episodeName: 03/26/21 / The original anti-vaxxer (from The Atlantic’s The Experiment podcast)
text: Over the years, people keep reaching back into Henning Jacobson’s case, looking for answers—not just to vaccination questions, but to bigger questions about how much power the government should have over our bodies.
